power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: The Quantitative Psychologist Is Dead, Long Live the Quantitative Psychologist

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychology
								National University of Singapore

text.text: Much of what quantitative psychologists publish consists of developing statistical methods, implementing them in software, and evaluating them in simulation studies.
I argue that artificial intelligence (AI) can already do much of this work, and that its share will only grow.
The quantitative psychologist has always been a jack of all trades, combining programming, statistics, and psychological knowledge without being a master of any one of them.
AI is now the better jack of all trades.
When methods become cheap, value moves to what AI cannot supply and to what it newly makes possible.

I describe three directions: collecting trustworthy data from real people, formalizing psychological theory now that computational modeling is within reach of any researcher, and rethinking methodological education so that students learn to judge the analyses that AI will run for them.
The specialist role built around producing methods for others will fade, while quantitative thinking spreads through all of psychology.

In May 2026, at the Annual Convention of the Association for Psychological Science in Barcelona, I attended a session in which a new model was presented that was theoretically interesting but could not yet be estimated from data.

While listening, I realized that the model shared much of its structure with models I had already implemented in my own software, so I asked an artificial intelligence (AI) coding agent to implement it.
This was easy to do: I have a dedicated laptop running AI coding agents, and I can prompt them directly from my phone.
By the end of the session, the agent had implemented the model, run preliminary simulations of its performance, and written a report on the results.
The quality of that preliminary report was acceptable, and no different from much of the work that appears in our top journals and that can take PhD students months to complete.

Much of what quantitative psychologists publish in journals such as Psychometrika, Psychological Methods, and Multivariate Behavioral Research consists of developing a statistical method, implementing it in software, and evaluating it in a simulation study.

In a review of 321 articles published in Psychological Methods, Behavior Research Methods, and Multivariate Behavioral Research in 2021 and 2022, nearly a third reported a simulation study (Siepe et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In a review of 321 articles published in Psychological Methods, Behavior Research Methods, and Multivariate Behavioral Research in 2021 and 2022, nearly a third reported a simulation study <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Siepe et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This kind of work is the business model of our field: we justify our positions, grants, and PhD projects by producing new methods, software, and simulation evidence.
Not all quantitative psychology fits this description, but much of what fills our journals does.
I argue that this business model is coming to an end, and I expect that within five years most such work will be done mainly by AI.

I distinguish the quantitative psychologist as a specialist, whose role is built around producing methods for others to use, from quantitative psychology as the broader endeavor of bringing rigorous quantitative thinking to psychological questions.
The first will fade, and the second will flourish.
I describe three directions in which we, and psychology as a whole, can move forward: collecting trustworthy data, formalizing psychological theory, and rethinking methodological education.
These are not only concerns for methodologists.
If I am right, every empirical researcher now has, or soon will have, an expert methodologist at hand, and with it the responsibility to judge what that methodologist produces.
Psychology has always needed methods of its own.
When Spearman (1904) set out to measure intelligence in schoolchildren, he had to develop what became factor analysis to make sense of his data.
text.formatted: When <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Spearman (1904)</ref> set out to measure intelligence in schoolchildren, he had to develop what became factor analysis to make sense of his data.

text.text: For a long time, methodological and empirical work went hand in hand.
But the methods grew more technical, and the mathematical training in psychology curricula did not keep pace (Borsboom, 2006).
text.formatted: But the methods grew more technical, and the mathematical training in psychology curricula did not keep pace <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Borsboom, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: A separate specialization emerged, with its own societies, journals, and doctoral programs, training a different kind of psychologist: the quantitative psychologist.

Not even two decades ago, a task force of the American Psychological Association worried that there were too few of us: in 2003, fewer than 30 doctorates were awarded in quantitative psychology, against 1,221 in clinical psychology (American Psychological Association, 2009, p. 11).
text.formatted: Not even two decades ago, a task force of the American Psychological Association worried that there were too few of us: in 2003, fewer than 30 doctorates were awarded in quantitative psychology, against 1,221 in clinical psychology <ref type="bibr">(American Psychological Association, 2009, p. 11)</ref>.

text.text: AI is about to solve that shortage, and then some.
Over time, the specialization and the researchers it was meant to serve grew apart.

Of the articles published in six prominent psychology journals in 2005 and 2006, 39% did not cite a single quantitative methodology source (Mills et al., 2010). Sharpe (2013) described a communication gap between methodologists and empirical researchers, and Borsboom (2006) observed that the way psychologists analyzed their tests in 2006 bore an "uncanny resemblance" to that of the 1950s (p. 425).
text.formatted: Of the articles published in six prominent psychology journals in 2005 and 2006, 39% did not cite a single quantitative methodology source <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Mills et al., 2010)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Sharpe (2013)</ref> described a communication gap between methodologists and empirical researchers, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Borsboom (2006)</ref> observed that the way psychologists analyzed their tests in 2006 bore an "uncanny resemblance" to that of the 1950s (p. 425).

text.text: The gap runs both ways: many empirical researchers do not cite our work, and much of our work, I would argue, is written by quantitative psychologists for quantitative psychologists.
Today, it is possible to obtain a PhD in quantitative psychology without ever meeting a research participant.
I know, because I did.
What made the quantitative psychologist valuable was a combination of skills.
We can program well enough to write software that many researchers use.
We know more mathematics and statistics than most psychologists.
And we understand psychological data and the questions that empirical researchers ask of them.
None of these skills is exceptional on its own.
We are not trained programmers: methodologists "typically lack formal training in programming and engineering software" (Epskamp, 2019, p. 151).
text.formatted: We are not trained programmers: methodologists "typically lack formal training in programming and engineering software" <ref type="bibr">(Epskamp, 2019, p. 151)</ref>.

text.text: We are rarely the strongest statisticians or mathematicians, and our knowledge of a psychological subfield seldom matches that of its specialists.
The quantitative psychologist is a jack of all trades and a master of none.
For decades, that combination made the best of us what Sharpe (2013) called Mavens: the colleagues whom researchers "seek out when their data need analyzing" (p. 577).
text.formatted: For decades, that combination made the best of us what <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Sharpe (2013)</ref> called Mavens: the colleagues whom researchers "seek out when their data need analyzing" (p. 577).

text.text: AI is now the better jack of all trades.

In my experience, it already programs better than most of us, covers more statistics and mathematics than any one of us, and knows enough psychology to connect these technical skills to psychological data and questions.
Every empirical researcher now has a Maven available at any hour, one that never has to be asked twice.
My experience in Barcelona proves little on its own, and I was well placed for it: the model resembled ones in my own software, and I could judge the output.
But for methods like this one, the bottleneck was rarely the idea.
It was the implementation, and that bottleneck is disappearing.
This also says something uncomfortable about the work itself.
If an AI agent can produce, within a single conference session, a preliminary report comparable to much of our published work, then that work is more routine than we like to admit.
My own work is no exception.
For a while, this will feel like a golden age, and in many ways it will be one.
Methods now locked behind paywalls and commercial software will be reimplemented in open-source alternatives.
Models that have been proposed but never implemented will become available.
We will learn many new things about the methods we use now.
The familiar answer "it can be done in principle, but. . . " will be replaced by "sure, let's do it."
We will tell ourselves that AI is a tool and that we remain in charge: we are the project leaders, and AI is our tireless research assistant.
This arrangement will not last.
Sooner or later, someone will instruct an AI to read the methodological literature, identify an open problem, develop and implement a solution, evaluate it, write the paper, and submit it.
A first version of this has already happened.

In machine learning, the developers of an AI system selected three manuscripts that it had produced without human modification and submitted them to a workshop at a major conference; one passed the first round of peer review (Lu et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In machine learning, the developers of an AI system selected three manuscripts that it had produced without human modification and submitted them to a workshop at a major conference; one passed the first round of peer review <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Lu et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The workshop accepted 70% of submissions, the paper was withdrawn as planned, and by its developers' own assessment none of the papers met the bar for the main conference.
Psychology is not machine learning, but the trajectory is hard to miss.
Journals that follow the guidance of the Committee on Publication Ethics (2023) do not accept AI as an author, because an author must take responsibility for the work.
When the AI does the methodological research and the human signs for it, the human's remaining contribution is accountability.
Whether accountability alone can sustain a scientific discipline is a question we will soon have to answer, and we may start to wonder whether we are prompting the AI or the AI is prompting us.
The obvious objection is that someone has to check what the AI produces, and that this someone is us.
I take the objection seriously, but it does not save the specialist.

First, the comparison is not with flawless human methodologists: the software that accompanies methodological work can have its own bugs, and the empirical researchers who use it cannot be expected to check it (Epskamp, 2019, pp. 151-152).
text.formatted: First, the comparison is not with flawless human methodologists: the software that accompanies methodological work can have its own bugs, and the empirical researchers who use it cannot be expected to check it <ref type="bibr">(Epskamp, 2019, pp. 151-152)</ref>.

text.text: Second, in my experience AI can already test its own code against known special cases and simulated data at a scale that no human reviewer would attempt.
It can still be confidently wrong (Lu et al., 2026), so independent checks, by another model or by a person, remain essential.
text.formatted: It can still be confidently wrong <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Lu et al., 2026)</ref>, so independent checks, by another model or by a person, remain essential.

text.text: Third, the check that matters most is whether an analysis suits the data and the question, and that depends more on understanding both than on developing methods.
A few experts will remain to arbitrate hard cases, but arbitration alone does not sustain a specialization.
Verification will become a skill that every researcher needs.
In general, AI will augment psychological research rather than replace it (Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2026): a human still decides what to ask and what to believe.
text.formatted: In general, AI will augment psychological research rather than replace it <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2026)</ref>: a human still decides what to ask and what to believe.

text.text: However, acting on those decisions will no longer require a methods specialist.

When producing methods becomes cheap, value moves to what AI cannot supply, such as data from real people and the judgment to evaluate output, and to what it newly makes possible, such as formal theory.
I see three directions.
Psychology studies the behavior and experience of people, and that requires data from people.

When collected online from unverified respondents, such data are becoming harder to trust. Westwood (2025) built an AI agent that completed online surveys while maintaining a consistent human persona.
text.formatted: When collected online from unverified respondents, such data are becoming harder to trust. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Westwood (2025)</ref> built an AI agent that completed online surveys while maintaining a consistent human persona.

text.text: It passed 99.8% of 6,000 standard attention checks and could infer a researcher's hypotheses and produce data that confirmed them.
In his words, "the foundational assumption of survey research-that a coherent response is a human response-is no longer tenable" (Westwood, 2025, p. 1).
text.formatted: In his words, "the foundational assumption of survey research-that a coherent response is a human response-is no longer tenable" <ref type="bibr">(Westwood, 2025, p. 1)</ref>.

text.text: AI can produce plausible responses, but we study people because we want their responses.
Even Centaur, a model that predicts human choices in experiments it was not trained on, was built from the trialby-trial data of more than 60,000 participants in 160 experiments (Binz et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Even Centaur, a model that predicts human choices in experiments it was not trained on, was built from the trialby-trial data of more than 60,000 participants in 160 experiments <ref type="bibr">(Binz et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A model trained on past behavior can generalize from it, but whether its predictions hold for a new population, a new intervention, or a changing world can ultimately only be checked against new data from people.
Data collected from verified human participants, in the lab, in the clinic, and in longrunning cohorts, will therefore become more valuable than ever.
The form of these data may change.
We may stop asking people to rate statements on 5-point scales and instead let them answer in their own words, with AI turning words into numbers (see Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2026).
text.formatted: We may stop asking people to rate statements on 5-point scales and instead let them answer in their own words, with AI turning words into numbers (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: But the words must come from a person.
I expect the most impactful work in psychology to be the collection of new, trustworthy data.
For quantitative psychologists, this means that study design, sampling, and measurement (the parts of methodology closest to the participant) will matter most.
Detecting synthetic respondents is itself a measurement problem, and one we are well placed to work on.
AI also changes what empirical researchers can do technically.

Formal models of psychological phenomena, such as a computational model of panic disorder (Robinaugh et al., 2024) or the formalized clinical case conceptualization that my colleagues and I proposed (Burger et al., 2020), have so far required expertise in dynamical systems and programming that few psychologists have.
text.formatted: Formal models of psychological phenomena, such as a computational model of panic disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Robinaugh et al., 2024)</ref> or the formalized clinical case conceptualization that my colleagues and I proposed <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Burger et al., 2020)</ref>, have so far required expertise in dynamical systems and programming that few psychologists have.

text.text: That barrier is disappearing.
A researcher who can describe a theory in words can now ask an AI to translate it into equations, simulate it, and compare its behavior with data.
We may see psychological theories formalized on a scale not seen before.
What AI removes is the excuse.
Formalizing a theory exposes the assumptions that verbal theories leave implicit (Guest & Martin, 2021).
text.formatted: Formalizing a theory exposes the assumptions that verbal theories leave implicit <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Guest & Martin, 2021</ref>).

text.text: An AI that silently fills these gaps produces a model without improving the theory, so deciding what the model should say remains the researcher's job.
What changes is that "I do not know how to build such a model" is no longer a reason not to try.

This points to a different future from the one that Yuan et al. (2026, p. 6) envision for 2050, in which a "Great Decoupling" makes theory construction its own specialization and theorists no longer test their own theories.
AI makes the opposite feasible: one researcher, aided by AI, can formalize a theory, collect the data to test it, and analyze the results.

There are good reasons to separate those who propose theories from those who test them, but AI pulls toward a recoupling of the theorist, the methodologist, and the empiricist, the combination that Spearman embodied.
Psychology itself will not disappear, because the need to understand human behavior will not go away, and psychology is arguably the most complex science there is.
As psychologists, we study more than eight billion people, each a complex system with their own genes, upbringing, experiences, values, and culture.
These systems interact, and they change in response to how they are studied and described.
AI is now changing how people work, learn, and relate to one another, raising questions that did not exist a few years ago.
I expect AI to settle the great open problems of mathematics, and to help find a cure for cancer, long before it truly understands human behavior.
Psychology programs will therefore continue to train clinicians, school psychologists, human resource professionals, policy advisors, and researchers.

All of them need to understand how research is designed, what makes a measurement valid, and how to interpret a statistical result, and they need this more than before, because they will spend their careers evaluating analyses that an AI ran for them.

The same AI that is a tireless Maven for researchers is a tireless tutor for students, so what teachers add is less explanation than judgment: setting problems in which the plausible answer is wrong, assessing the reasoning rather than the output, and vouching that a student can do this without help.
Our teaching should move from how to run an analysis to how to judge one.
AI also gives us better tools for this.
Building an in-class experiment, an interactive simulation, or a large set of exercises used to require, at least for me, a software team; now it takes me an evening.
I share several such tools on a platform I built for sharing educational mini-apps: Galvoro (galvoro.app).
For example, one of them lets students arrange two groups of balls until their difference is statistically significant and then explore power and false-positive rates through simulation.
The specialist will fade, but quantitative work itself is becoming universal.

When every psychologist has an expert methodologist at their disposal, every psychologist can become a quantitative psychologist: one who collects data with care, formalizes theory, and judges models.
AI may thus achieve what our specialization set out to do, bringing rigorous methods to all of psychology, by making the specialization itself unnecessary.
This has practical consequences.
PhD students in our field should still learn statistics and programming, if only to check what AI produces, but they should also learn to collect data, to build theories, and to teach.
Departments should hire methodologists with these broader skills and make the evaluation of AI-generated analyses an explicit goal of the curriculum.
Journals will likely have to raise the bar for the methodological papers they publish.
The quantitative psychologist as we now know it will disappear and become instead a role that every psychologist can take on.
The endeavor of studying human behavior and cognition with rigorous quantitative methods will remain, and it will matter more than ever.
The quantitative psychologist is dead, long live the quantitative psychologist.
